ak_southeastern_alaska_coastal_range.blurb: Southeast Alaska stretches from the northern Coast Range down the panhandle, a rainforest region where granite peaks mix with volcanic, heavily forested islands. Juneau holds the largest share, with small road-system crags, the Mendenhall Towers as the most developed alpine objective, and granite cliffs reachable only by boat. Skagway adds granite trad. Sitka, Haines and Ketchikan are smaller. The climbing is varied: trad and bouldering lead, with sport, alpine and ice mixed in. Roped grades mostly sit between 5.8 and 5.11. Rain is the main factor, and a local gym is the fallback. Alaska's general climbing season runs May through September.

wv_seneca_rocks.blurb: Seneca Rocks is a long fin of white-to-gray Tuscarora quartzite in West Virginia's Monongahela National Forest, with the layers tilted nearly upright. Climbing is overwhelmingly traditional multipitch, with only a small number of bolted lines, and the grading is stiff. Routes run from easy fifth class to 5.13, with the bulk between 5.7 and 5.11; vertical cracks give good protection. Most descents involve rappels, so wear a helmet because rockfall is a real concern. The West Face stays shaded until early afternoon while the East Face is sunny until late afternoon. South Peak, North Peak, the Lower Slabs and Southern Pillar are the main sections. Climbing is generally possible from spring through fall.

az_beardsley_boulders_area.blurb: Beardsley sits on a desert peak in north Phoenix, a hillside strewn with coarse, weathered granite boulders. Bouldering makes up the great majority of the climbing, with a smaller set of trad and sport routes on larger formations up the slope. Problems range from easy scrambles to about V9, with most between V0 and V5. Heights reach around 15 feet, so bring a pad, and expect old-school grading that can feel harder than the number. Phoenix is mainly a winter destination with a long summer, which suits a quick session in the cooler months. Beardsley Bouldering is the main part, with Beardsley Roped Routes covering the rope climbs.

ca_outback_the_2.blurb: The Outback is a large spread of rock formations in Joshua Tree National Park, north of Hidden Valley, at about 4,200 feet. Approaches are short, often 5 to 10 minutes. Trad dominates, with a lot of cracks and faces, plus plenty of bouldering scattered around, top-ropes and very little sport. Grades run from easy fifth class to 5.13, with the bulk of roped climbs at 5.7 to 5.11, and boulder problems up to about V8. The area stretches from Steve Canyon in the west, where sheltered canyon walls hold many quality routes, east toward Echo Cove and north to Dutzi Rock.

mn_blue_mounds_state_park_luverne.blurb: Blue Mounds is a state park in the far southwest of Minnesota, near Luverne, where pink Sioux quartzite cliffs rise about 100 feet above tallgrass prairie. The colour comes from iron oxide. Most climbs are 50 to 60 feet tall, and there are no bolted routes: it is trad, top-rope and a good deal of bouldering. Roped grades span 5.4 to 5.12, mostly 5.8 to 5.10, and problems run mostly V0 to V4. Climbing is spread over the South Quarry, North Quarry, Prairie Walls and Mini Fortress areas. Snow can linger behind the Prairie Wall into late April.

ak_fairbanks_and_vicinity.blurb: This covers rock and ice in the immediate vicinity of Fairbanks, in Alaska's Interior. Bouldering is the biggest share, with sport, trad, top-rope and some ice and alpine. Grapefruit Rocks, limestone about 50 miles north of town, is the largest area, holding most of the sport and top-rope climbing. Granite Tors are granite buttresses above tree line, mostly trad, with a long and remote approach. Bouldering is concentrated at Tatlanika, Sheep Creek and Savage River. Roped grades mostly run 5.7 to 5.11 and boulder problems from V0 to about V7, and several creeks hold ice routes.
